newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Failed Malaysia bank talks won't dent industry.
newsitem.headline: Failed Malaysia bank talks won't dent industry.

text.p: The failure of two major Malaysian banking groups to reach decisions on mergers would not affect the financial industry as a whole, analysts said.

Singapore's Overseas-Chinese Banking Corporation said in a statement on Friday that the proposed merger between its Malaysian unit and Malaysia's Pacific Bank Bhd had been terminated because of complex legal and accounting issues.

Meanwhile, Malaysian Industrial Development Finance Bhd (MIDF) said in a separate statement it "does not intend to dispose of its equity interest in Oriental Bank Bhd. Malaysian conglomerate Sime Darby had announced it was planning to buy a 51 percent equity stake in Oriental.

"It's a minor setback. The deals may probably still go through, but it's a question of finding the best fit. It may require 'Big Brother' (Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara) forcing everyone to come back to the negotiating table," said Angie Ang, banking analyst at Caspian Research (Malaysia).
"The two deals failed for different reasons," said another banking analyst at a foreign equities research house in Kuala Lumpur.

"With OCBC it was an issue of control. With MIDF, Permodalan Nasional Bhd (the state-owned investment fund and major shareholder of MIDF) was concerned that MIDF would not be left with much if they sold off Oriental," he added.
The analyst said OCBC's investors were likely to greet the news positively, but it was not good news for Pacific Bank.
"The news means that Pacific Bank's net tangible assets will now be lower than was expected, but it would have meant that OCBC would have lost management control of Pacific Bank," he said.

Analysts said the attraction for Pacific in the planned merger was a larger branch network and a tie-up with a regional bank. "It's slightly negative as there was a lot of expectations. Pacific stocks should come off as a lot of people expect it to go through," said another banking analyst.
The effect of the move on MIDF's share price should be positive, analysts said, because it would retain control of a valuable asset. "Oriental is seen as a jewel," Ang said.
The impact on Sime Darby, however, was likely to be generally negative, said analysts. "Sime's share price may be hit some more," one analyst said.
Malaysia's central bank has been trying to consolidate the local banking industry for the past two years, in the face of market deregulation which should start to take effect by 2005.
In May, the Malaysian operations of OCBC and Pacific Bank announced their plans to merge, marking the first of several such deals.

In November, Malaysia's largest stockbroking house Rashid Hussain Bhd announced plans to acquire a controlling stake in Kwong Yik Bank for 2.16 billion ringgit, and merge it with its own DCB Bank Bhd, a unit of DCB Holdings Bhd.
In December, Sime Darby entered the fray with its plans to acquire a 51 percent stake in Oriental Bank.
"These banks don't want to let go unless they push the prices to the limit," Ang said. "Reality is setting in." ($1 = 2.49 ringgit) -- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
